title: The bridge
hook: stones float with Rama's name on them; the squirrel carries sand
carry: the name of god carries what would sink

segments.voice: Yesterday: the search, and Sampati, who gave his dead brother water before he gave his news. Tarpan.
screen: `TARPAN: THE DEAD ARE REMEMBERED WITH WATER.`

segments.voice: Hanuman has leapt the ocean, found Sita, given her the ring, and set Lanka on fire. Now he's back, and the whole army stands on India's southern shore looking at the problem. Hanuman can leap the ocean. A whole monkey army can't. Rama sits on the beach for three days, in Valmiki's telling, asking the ocean to let them pass. The ocean doesn't answer. So Rama, furious, picks up his bow and aims an arrow at the sea itself. And the ocean rises out of the water, in person, and says: don't dry me up. There's another way.
screen: `AN ARMY AT THE EDGE OF THE SEA.` → `THREE DAYS, NO ANSWER.` → `RAMA AIMS AT THE OCEAN.`

segments.voice: The ocean god tells Rama that one of his monkeys, Nala, is the son of the builder of the gods, and can build a bridge the sea will hold up. So the army goes to work. They tear up trees, boulders and whole rocky hilltops, carry them to the water, and Nala lays them in a line. In Valmiki it takes five days to reach Lanka. People call it Rama Setu. Setu means bridge: Rama's bridge. Then the tellings most people grew up on add the part everyone remembers. Before each stone goes in, the monkeys write one word on it: Rama. And the stones float. Rocks that should sink stay up, because they carry the name. An old Hindi saying puts it simply: Ram se bada Ram ka naam. Greater than Rama is Rama's name. This is a big Hindu teaching about nama, the name of God. The name isn't just a label; for devotees, it carries the one it names. It's why Hindus repeat it on beads, japa, from day thirteen. It's why some fill whole notebooks writing it by hand, a practice called likhita japa, written repetition. And in those same tellings, a little squirrel rolls in the sand and shakes it between the stones, over and over. A monkey nearly steps on it. Rama picks it up and strokes its back with three fingers; the Indian palm squirrel's three pale stripes, people say, are where he touched it. Nobody in that army could make a rock float. They could only write the name on it, and trust it.
screen: `NALA LAYS THE STONES.` · `EACH STONE CARRIES ONE NAME: RAMA.` · `RAM SE BADA RAM KA NAAM.` · `NAMA: THE NAME CARRIES THE ONE IT NAMES.` · `A SQUIRREL, THREE STRIPES.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper. Slowly write a name of God you love, Ram, or Shri Ram, or another, eleven times, one under the other, and say it under your breath as you write. If you don't pray, write one word you'd want to lean on when things feel heavy. Then look at the page. That's likhita japa: a name written down so you can lean on it.
Rama Setu. Rama's bridge: stones that float because they carry his name, with a squirrel filling the gaps.
Your line: the name of God carries what would sink. Ram se bada Ram ka naam. Tomorrow, Ravana's court.

howItsDone: Many Hindus repeat Rama's name on beads, and some fill notebooks writing it by hand (likhita japa). Rameswaram, on the Tamil Nadu coast, is an important pilgrimage place linked to the building of the bridge; the chain of shoals between India and Sri Lanka is often called Rama Setu, and the squirrel story is a favorite told to children.

nama.meaning: the name of God, held as sacred in itself

likhita japa.meaning: repeating God's name by writing it by hand
